Listen to this article Share Nigeria’s youthful population will not automatically become an economic dividend. It will do so only when young people can find productive work, build viable businesses, acquire relevant skills and influence the policies that determine their prospects. The country’s challenge is not simply to prepare its young people for the economy as it exists but to build an economy capable of putting their abilities to productive use. That requires enterprise and politics to work together. The cost of failing to make this connection is already visible. The National Bureau of Statistics’ Nigeria Labour Force Survey for the first quarter of 2024 found that 14.4 percent of Nigerians aged 15 to 24 were not in employment, education or training, up from 13.7 percent in the third quarter of 2023. The survey also put youth unemployment at 8.4 percent. These indicators measure different aspects of labour-market exclusion, but together they underline the need to examine not just whether young people have jobs, but whether they have access to education, training and pathways into productive economic activity. Nigeria’s young people are not waiting passively for opportunity. They are establishing technology businesses, running farms, producing films and music, building fashion brands and providing services. Their initiative demonstrates considerable entrepreneurial capacity. Indeed, ambition cannot compensate indefinitely for unreliable infrastructure, expensive credit, inconsistent regulation and weak access to markets. A promising business can struggle not because its founder lacks ideas, but because the conditions for turning those ideas into sustainable enterprises remain inadequate. The implications extend beyond individual businesses. According to the 2021 Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Survey by the Small and Medium Enterprises Development Agency of Nigeria and the National Bureau of Statistics, micro, small and medium-sized enterprises contributed approximately 46.32 percent of Nigeria’s gross domestic product and accounted for 87.9 percent of employment. Although these figures are based on a 2021 survey and should not be mistaken for current estimates, they demonstrate the importance of smaller businesses to the national economy. If Nigeria wants more productive jobs for young people, it must make it easier for such enterprises to survive, formalise, expand and employ workers. This is where politics becomes inseparable from enterprise. Electricity prices and reliability affect production costs. Roads and transport networks determine how quickly goods reach customers. Tax administration, trade rules and regulatory consistency influence business planning. Access to finance determines whether entrepreneurs can purchase equipment, expand operations or withstand temporary setbacks. Housing and urban planning affect whether workers can live within a reasonable distance of employment. These conditions are shaped, to varying degrees, by decisions made at federal, state and local levels. The World Bank’s business indicators illustrate the scale of one such constraint. Its data show that 82 percent of firms in Nigeria experienced electrical outages in 2025. This is a measure of how widespread the problem is, not the proportion of electricity demand left unmet, but it reinforces the burden unreliable supply places on businesses. For a small manufacturer, a food processor or a digital services company, interruptions can mean lost production, damaged goods, missed deadlines and additional expenditure on alternative power. Entrepreneurs can improve their own efficiency, but they cannot individually reform the electricity market or build the national infrastructure on which their competitiveness depends. Young entrepreneurs therefore have a legitimate interest in public policy. Indeed, too many discussions of enterprise treat political participation as a separate civic responsibility, something to attend to during election campaigns and set aside when business resumes. This separation is costly. When business owners do not engage with policy, decisions affecting their costs, access to finance and prospects for growth are left largely to others. Participation does not guarantee good policy, but organised, evidence-based engagement gives citizens a better chance of influencing it. Nigeria’s political participation figures also deserve attention. In remarks delivered in February 2026, the Independent National Electoral Commission reported that turnout in presidential elections fell from 53.7 percent of registered voters in 2011 to 26.7 percent in 2023. Turnout alone does not explain why citizens abstain, and low participation cannot be attributed exclusively to young voters. Nevertheless, the decline raises questions about public confidence, political representation and the ability of elections to sustain meaningful engagement between citizens and their leaders. The answer is not to tell every young Nigerian to become a politician. Enterprise itself is a form of economic participation, and businesses need people focused on building products, serving customers and creating employment. But entrepreneurs, professionals, farmers and creative workers should also recognise that their collective interests deserve representation in policy discussions. Business associations, professional bodies, cooperatives and youth-led organisations can help translate individual frustrations into proposals that governments can assess and implement. Such engagement must be specific. Rather than merely demanding cheaper electricity, business associations should press for published service-performance data, transparent tariff decisions and enforceable standards for electricity providers. Rather than requesting general support for small businesses, they should advocate for simpler registration and tax compliance, predictable regulatory requirements and transparent reporting on public credit schemes. Rather than calling for more youth employment, they should demand programmes that disclose how many people obtain jobs, how many remain employed after a year and how much public expenditure each sustained job costs. The government must respond with equally measurable commitments. Federal and state administrations should publish annual targets for reducing administrative delays, expanding reliable infrastructure and improving access to productive finance. Publicly supported enterprise programmes should disclose beneficiaries, expenditure, repayment performance where applicable, and independently assessed employment outcomes. Training initiatives should be linked to employers and verified demand for skills, rather than judged primarily by enrolment or certificates issued. These measures would make it easier for citizens to distinguish effective interventions from announcements that generate publicity without lasting economic value. Political parties also have responsibilities. They should provide credible routes for younger members to contribute to policy development, compete for leadership and demonstrate their capabilities. Transparent candidate-selection procedures, internal accountability and published policy proposals would offer a stronger basis for participation than appeals to age or generational identity alone. Young politicians, in turn, must demonstrate competence, integrity and a willingness to be judged by results. Being young is not itself evidence of sound judgement, just as experience does not automatically confer wisdom. There is also a responsibility within the business community. Entrepreneurs must invest in skills, improve productivity, comply with legitimate obligations and create working environments that offer employees opportunities to develop. Businesses cannot demand accountability from government while ignoring their own responsibilities to workers, customers and the public. Nor should every commercial failure be blamed on politics; weak business models, inadequate market research and poor management can also undermine promising ventures. A productive economy requires capable enterprises as well as capable public institutions. Nigeria’s youth dividend will emerge only when these responsibilities reinforce one another. Young people need the skills and freedom to build enterprises; businesses need reliable infrastructure, finance and predictable rules; and citizens need institutions that listen, disclose information and respond to legitimate demands. None of these conditions can substitute for the others. The task before Nigeria is therefore larger than encouraging young people to start businesses or urging them to vote. It is to connect enterprise with accountable government so that economic initiative has a realistic chance of succeeding. The measure of progress should be whether more young Nigerians can build sustainable livelihoods, whether more businesses grow into productive employers and whether public policy responds to evidence rather than political convenience. A youthful population is an opportunity, not a guarantee. Turning it into a dividend will require both the enterprise to create value and the political will to build the conditions that allow that value to endure. Arc. Felix O. Arome is an architect and entrepreneur with a keen interest in national development, youth leadership and African enterprise.
